source_context:
Change ringing: Stedman's plain changes as a verified extent. English tower bells cannot be rung to a melody; what is rung is a sequence of rows, orderings of the bells, in which consecutive rows differ by swapping adjacent positions. The module defines AdjSwap (two lists differ by one swap of adjacent entries), the block hunt a b r in which a new bell is inserted into every position of a row r in one of the two directions, and rows l, the plain changes on the start row l, built by letting the first bell hunt alternately through the extent on the remaining bells. The declared results are the extent properties: rows l has (length l)! entries, contains a row exactly when it is a permutation of l, has no repeated row when l has no repeated bell, begins with l, and satisfies IsChain AdjSwap, so consecutive rows differ by one adjacent transposition. The construction was published by Fabian Stedman (Campanalogia, 1677) and rediscovered as the Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter enumeration; the mathematics is classical and only its absence from the baseline is claimed.

Motivation. The operator asked for a subject reached from an unexpected angle and chose bell ringing from a shortlist the agent proposed. The theorem is why seventeenth-century ringers could ring a full extent at all, three centuries before the literature on Gray codes for permutations.

Absence evidence over the pinned Mathlib tree at v4.33.0-rc1. The strings change ringing, Steinhaus (outside Banach-Steinhaus), Johnson, Trotter, plain changes, and Gray code occur nowhere relevant: no Hamiltonicity of a Cayley graph of the symmetric group under adjacent transpositions, no ordered enumeration of permutations with a step invariant. What Mathlib has is reused rather than duplicated: List.permutations'Aux performs the insertions, mem_permutations', nodup_permutations, length_permutations and permutations_perm_permutations' give counting and coverage, and the List.IsChain API carries the step invariant. In the LeanFrontier corpus the GroupTheory subject directory was previously empty.

Implementation. rows l is a permutation of List.permutations' l, by induction, because each hunt block is a permutations'Aux block or its reverse; length, membership and nodup transfer along that permutation, so counting and coverage cost nothing new. The chain result is the real content: within a block, successive insertions of the hunting bell differ by carrying it past one resident bell, by induction with isChain_map; at a junction between blocks the hunting bell stands still at the front or the back while the rows beneath it differ by the inductively known change, handled by the congruence lemmas adjSwap_cons and adjSwap_concat and by closed forms for the first and last entries of a block. The direction is a Bool rather than an index, which keeps every induction structural. Imports are four files.

Verification beyond the receiver. The same construction was written independently in Python, mirroring permutations'Aux line by line, and checked for every number of bells from one to seven: factorial length, no repeated row, exact coverage of all permutations, first row equal to the start row, and every consecutive pair an adjacent swap; 5040 rows on seven bells, no violation. This guards against a wrong definition proved consistent with itself, which the receiver cannot detect.

Not included. The parity alternation of consecutive rows, the cyclic closure back to the start row, the methods with several simultaneous swaps per change (plain hunt, Plain Bob, Stedman's method), and the Cayley-graph reading are each left to their own submission.

Provenance. Produced from the repository TRY-LEANFRONTIER launcher, same agent as the josephus-survivor-binary-shift and bounded-slope-greatest-minorant submissions. The shortlist, statements, proofs, and the decision to submit were the agent's; the operator picked the subject. Proofs use structural induction and the List.IsChain and Perm API by name, with no numeric automation.
